utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Interpreters. I say good morning to the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. Let us resume, Mr. Nobilo. Have you found your witness, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. He was waiting for us in the hotel and he's ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Before he comes in, just a minute. Mr. Dubuisson, do you have the little introduction to the witness? In that case, there will be no need for an oral summary. So if Mr. Dubuisson could give me this piece of paper. It is a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is a witness for whom the Defence is going to request a pseudonym, and it will be DL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: While the registrar is looking for it, we can have Witness DL brought in to avoid wasting time. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to call you DL. It is a pseudonym as you are going to enjoy protective measures granted by the Court, requested by the Defence. Please verify that that is your name that the registrar is going to show you without repeating it, please. Remain standing for a few more minutes to make your solemn declaration that is going to be handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the established rules, we are going to call you Witness DL. You may be seated. The Defence counsel for the accused, the accused being here present, General Blaskic, General now, Colonel at the time, is going to ask you questions and he will explain to you how the procedure will go on: First, questions by the Defence, and then the Prosecution, and then the Judges. So Mr. Nobilo, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please move into a private session just for a few minutes in order to ascertain a few things about this witness in terms of his CV?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D432.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first subject that we asked you to testify about are the events in Dusina. So could you please show the Court on this map where Dusina is, in which municipality, and what are the localities surrounding Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, here, approximately, about 15 kilometres away from Zenica towards Lasva, and from Lasva, about 3 kilometres to Busovaca, so this is the area between Busovaca and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dusina belongs to the municipality of Zenica but it's at the border towards Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does belong to the municipality of Zenica, but as a Catholic parish, it belongs to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who lived in this particular village? What was the ethnic composition of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a mixed community. In the lower part towards the main road was the Bosniak part of the village, and further up, about 400 or 500 metres away, were the Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DL, I should like to ask you that when you are answering the questions of Mr. Nobilo, that you face the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you please concentrate now on the 26th of January, 1993. Where were you then and is that the first time that you heard about the events in Dusina? Could you please explain this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 26th of January, 1993, I was at my regular job at the Croat house in Zenica as technical secretary of the HDZ. Around 12.00, in the hallway, in the anteroom to our offices, we heard people shouting, crying, and a lot of people came, and we walked out to see what was going on. A group of elderly people came, men and women and children, crying out of their wits and they were all saying that they were attacked, that their houses were torched, that there were people who were killed and wounded, and, of course, we couldn't hear what they were saying because they were all taking at the same time. We tried to calm them down. We took them away one by one. We first gave them some refreshments so that they could calm down. They were crying, they were pulling their hair, they were wondering what was happening to their nearest and dearest, and then they spoke to us and told us what had happened and we wrote down their complaints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please try to stop at the end of every sentence so that we can have a faithful interpretation of what you are saying? So there were some 50 desperate civilians who came in and who were all speaking at the same time and then you took statements from them. Could you explain to the Court now, what did you actually find out? How could you summarise these statements? What happened on the 26th of January, 1993, in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we put all of this together and when people calmed down a bit, we got the impression that a terrible thing had happened in Dusina. There were some bad situations, and we weren't quite sure what had exactly happened, but apparently about ten people had been killed. There were a few people who were wounded too. One house had burned down completely. Some other houses were torched and their furniture and other belongings were thrown out of the house, and that was the first time in that area that armed soldiers of the BH army did something like that to the civilian population, and this really astounded us. We didn't know what to do at first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, Witness DL, these Croats, these people who came to your office, these desperate people, were all of them Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, all of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they gave this description saying that ten people were killed, what did they say? Were they killed in fighting or were they executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what they said, that, first of all, in the morning, a group of armed soldiers came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the BH army. The BH army. And they asked them to say where members of the HVO from their village were. I don't know exactly how many of them were in the HVO. At that point in time, they didn't know where this was. But they sent someone to get them, and Mr. Zvonko Rajic, who was commander of this small HVO unit, came immediately with his friends, his comrades, these other soldiers, he came to surrender because they had threatened them saying that if they would not surrender, they would take rigorous measures against the civilian population if they did not show up within a given period of time. And then they said that Zvonko came with his comrades very quickly and they tied them up and took them behind the houses, and all these elderly men who opposed their actions were treated the same way. Soon after that, they heard shots, and they came to the conclusion that their nearest and dearest had been killed or wounded. They didn't know the exact number, but they had assumed, judging by the number of people who were tied up, that there were about ten persons who were killed. The rest fled. They came to Zenica terrified, frightened, at their wits end. But we have these traces of their experience in writing because we took this down, and I must say that we went to the exact location to see what had happened. What they said was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was their description? Was there looting of the houses? Did people rob these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that, first of all, they would burst into their houses and take the things that could easily be carried, like jewellery, gold, radio, TV sets, this technical equipment, and they took the furniture out of houses, they threw it out and they broke it with hammers, and they threw out everything that was in the houses, paintings from the walls, bed linen, and they tried to burn down the rest, and then they used RPGs and other firearms to shoot at houses so the windows were broken too, and they said that they could not imagine living in those houses anymore. They said, "They are trying to throw us out of this area because they were saying that they don't want to live with us." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, what is a Zolja, RPG, hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see from movies, it's some kind of a grenade that you put on a long gun, and then when it explodes, it can set a house on fire, it can destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please have a document distributed now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D433, D433A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, since we haven't got a French version, I would like to read this out. It's not a very long text. I would ask the witness to listen carefully and let us see whether this description matches what he then heard as well as later so ... Part of the text is a bit illegible, but we are going to try: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Jure Francetic brigade command. This is a report that was sent to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in Vitez. Subject: Report on the number of Croats from Lasva and the surrounding hamlets who were killed or captured. "On the basis of the report of a number of Croats from the villages of Dusina, Lasva local commune" -- it's quite illegible -- "there are quite a few people who are killed, wounded, or arrested on the basis of our most recent information. Please send us instructions regarding the funeral expenses for the executed soldiers because they were members of the Busovaca HVO." Below is the list of the individuals who were taken prisoner, wounded, missing, or executed. First of all, the executed, killed. Number 1, Franjo Rajic, Pero Rajic, Jozo Kegelj, Niko Kegelj, Vinko Kegelj, Stipo Kegelj (65 years old), Mladen Kegelj (tortured before being shot), Drazenko Kegelj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go on. I have the list in front of me. I see that there are twelve people who were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well, yes, yes, fine. Then there are those who were taken prisoner, a total of 30 of them, and two persons were missing, and three were wounded, and Commander Zivko Totic signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, these family names that you see here and the text that we just read out, does this match the information you basically received on that day, the 26th of January, 1993, and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This report was dated the 28th of January, which means two days after the statements made by the people who came to report this unhappy event to us and the attack on their village. In the first investigation, they did say that they didn't know the exact number of people who had been killed and wounded, because many people fled, and during that escape they were shot at and received their injuries. So they did not know the exact number of the killed and wounded, but what they saw with their own eyes, that is what they were able to tell us, those who were tied up and the shot, and those are the people they told us about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, according to your recollections, these names and surnames, are they the names of the individuals whom you were told had been killed, wounded or reported missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the surnames referred to the family name of Kegelj. There were some Rajics but they were most from the Kegelj family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you hand out another document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D434, D434A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm now going to read the main points from the text. This is a report from the Jure Francetic Brigade, sent to the command of the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia Operative Zone. It is the report on the massacre of Croats in the village of Dusina, the Lasva local commune. "On the 27th of January, 1992 (sic), displaced persons from the village of Dusina, Lasva local commune, arrived in Zenica and informed us of the massacre of Croats in the area mentioned." This is what is stated in the Jure Francetic report. "On the early morning of the 26th of January, 1993, the Muslim liberation forces (MOS) from Zenica surrounded seven Croatian houses in the village of Dusina. They demanded of Dusina HVO members that they surrender their weapons. After it was agreed that the demand would be honoured, MOS members opened fire on the Croatian houses. The shooting claimed the lives of the following individuals: Pero Rajic, Drazenko Kegelj and Franjo Rajic. During the negotiations, Zvonko Rajic was killed. "The following individuals were wounded: Marko Rajic and Blasko Bosnjak. The wounded were transported to the Zenica hospital. "After the shooting ceased, MOS members entered the village, closed the civilians in a house owned by Stipe Kegelj and kept them there until nightfall. They arrested the HVO soldiers and seized their weapons. "After that, they started searching the houses, threatening to shoot those who refused to surrender their weapons because they had been informed by the local Muslims that there were more weapons. As they were unable to find the weapons, they carried out the executions. "The following people were shot: Niko Kegelj, Vinko Kegelj, Jozo Kegelj, Mladenko Kegelj and August Rasod. "After the execution, the soldiers' bodies were taken to a cellar in the family house owned by Ivica and Jure Kegelj. "Because Marinko Kegelj managed to escape, his father, Stipo Kegelj, was executed instead. "The following people were reported missing, Perica Rados, Dragan Rados, Nedjeljko Rajic and Marinko Kegelj. "After having executed the HVO soldiers, the MOS members wanted to shoot Zdravka Rados, Dragan Rados's wife. It is assumed that they abandoned their idea to carry out the execution at the request of a local Muslim. "Ivica Kegelj and Marinko Rajic were beaten and subjected to maltreatment and then taken towards Zenica by the by the BH army Military Police." And it is signed by the brigade commander Zivko Totic. Tell me, witness DL, do you recognise the signature of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this report basically reflect your own knowledge, the information you received independently of the Jure Francetic Brigade, that is what the population of Dusina told you on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part it is the same. Of course, there are much more precise details in the report, and, of course, this is understandable because these people had time to collect themselves. They weren't as frightened as they were on the first day and under their initial impression, so they were able to state things in much greater detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Court now, please, prior to these events, in the area of the Lasva River Valley, Zenica, in this area, the area you lived in, Central Bosnia, before that event did any army ever storm the village and kill the civilians, any military units? Had this ever happened before on a previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the first instance. The first time that the -- that something of this kind happened in the surrounds of Zenica, that an armed force had stormed a civilian settlement and performed acts of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you ever hear previously that a military unit, either a Croat one or a Muslim one, had entered a civilian village and set fire to the houses there, before this event and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we never had reports that have kind. Perhaps somebody else had reports that have kind, but I never heard that in our vicinity, something like that had taken place. That was the first time, and it was so frightening and so terrible that we found it very difficult to tackle the situation, and see to the basic problems and help the population. We found it very difficult, because we didn't have any experience along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on the 26th of January, 1993, did the Croats and the Muslims, the HVO and the BH army, were they allies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And this communal spirit was reflected in the fact that in most villages where the settlements were of a mixed population, joint watches were set up in order to protect the households from the looting and pilfering that had been taking place because of the times we lived in. And so we wanted to prevent this looting of property, and we set up these joint watches. That's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, before this particular event, did you ever hear of any unit, HVO unit or BH army unit, an organised army unit, not a band of looters or pilferers, that they would storm the village and take away television sets, radios, jewellery, gold and anything that have kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we never heard of that kind of thing happening. This was the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After all these events, what are you doing with -- what did you do with the population? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as we were able, within the framework of our -- the possibilities open to us, we did everything to help the people, people who were not able to go home, who were frightened. So we sent them to Zenica and had them put up at relations' or anywhere else to try and mitigate this situation. And then we told them that the situation would calm down, and that when conditions returned to normal they would be able to go back to their homes, but not many people believed us after what had happened. But things did calm down, and by prominent individuals we tried to -- we contacted the official authorities of Zenica, and prevailed upon them to bring the situation back to normal, to ensure safety for these people and to adapt the houses for living quarters, but we were not able to come to terms with the Zenica authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you ever hear of any investigation being carried out, and that anybody was sent to prison because of what happened in Dusina? Did you hear of anything of that kind taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We insisted upon this from the HDZ. We wanted this to be publicised in the media in order to warn other villagers and other people living in the neighbourhood to beware of this. We asked the Zenica media, the press, the radio and television, to explain what had happened to the people, and to say that an investigation should be instigated against the perpetrators, but we never heard of this having happened or any results of any investigation of this kind. People, quite simply -- that is to say, the most responsible individuals said that this act was done by a unit out of their control, by a unit that they had not heard of, but that was not so. It was done by members of the BH army. They were the perpetrators, and we could see their badges on their arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when did you see the dead bodies for the first time and how did you come across them? Could you describe this to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, we were inquisitive, and we wanted to ascertain the truth, because in their first reports, people said that some people were killed with firearms, and we asked to go to the mortuary and see whether any of these bodies had been mutilated as people had previously said, to ascertain whether the rumours and stories of people from Dusina were true, but nobody wanted to hear anything about this. And I personally used an occasion whereby one of my neighbours was a guard in the mortuary, and I asked him whether the bodies killed in Dusina were in the mortuary and he told me that they were. He was good enough to enable me, in the evening hours, to go and look at the bodies and to ascertain whether stories that they had been -- knives had been used to kill them, and that they had been stabbed, to see whether this was true. So I went with two cameramen at about 7.00 in the evening, three days after the event. I went to the mortuary, to the morgue, and saw what I saw there. I kept the guard outside while the two cameramen filmed what they had seen, so that we could have a document of this particular scene, so that in the future we could ask for an investigation to be held with regard to this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the at one particular moment did you enter the morgue, and if so, what was your -- the greatest impression that you gained? What did you see upon entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really like to go into the morgue, because it is a terrible sight, but the young man -- the young cameraman told me to come in, and I talked to the guard outside, and he said, "Come in and see something for yourself." Then he used a battery to throw light on the scene. He took back the plastic covering, and one of the bodies -- there was a hole in one of the bodies, a real hole around about here, with a blunt object, made with a blunt object. I can only suppose that it was a knife. It was all black. You couldn't really see it, but the impression was that you could put a whole fist into the hole. That was how big it was. And I said, "Well, cover this up. I can't bear to look at this any longer," and they took pictures of this. I left the room and we only stayed there five minutes, not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The official -- the authorities didn't allow you do this, you did this secretly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, with regard to the hole on the body, what did you hear during the funeral, later on, from the father of Zvonko Rajic, who was the commander of the local HVO unit from the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we attended the funeral of the people who had been killed, in front of the church in Cajdras in Zenica there were about 3.000 mourners, people from the surrounding village and town. They had come to pay their last respects to the people that were killed. The father of the late Zvonko Rajic started crying in front of the body of his son, and he said, "Dear Zvonko, I can understand that they killed you, but why did they cut our heart out?" I couldn't -- I didn't really know what he meant, but when I remember the scene in the morgue, it might have been the hole in the chest, and that somehow the father of this young man had learnt of the terrible thing that they had done to his son in taking out his -- cutting out his heart. Perhaps he had a legal -- he was legally able to attend the abduction (sic) and was able to ascertain this during daylight, and was able to see this, and perhaps that is why he made the statement in front of so many people at the funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what Zvonko Rajic said coincided with what you saw on the body, and you do not know whose body it was at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, during the funeral itself, in front of the church in Cajdras, you said that there were 3.000 mourners. It was a mass funeral, a mass burial. Could you tell us the direction the funeral procession took and where the actual burial took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very strong impression that I gained in front of the church, because three people -- 3.000 people were crying, and it's -- it's a very strong impression. It was a terrible act that had happened for the first time in that area, and we were just not able to realise what had happened. But the mourners started out across Veternica and then towards Busovaca, and most of them, I think nine people were buried in Busovaca at that time, and they were all the parishioners of that particular parish, their parents, and nearest and dearest wanted them to be buried there, and most of the people, most of the mourners in Cajdras, went by bus to pay their last respects and to attend the burial, and I did myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Busovaca, was it the people of Busovaca that came out to pay their last respects? Were there a lot of people attending the funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The funeral lasted for a long time. It was almost up until dark, because everybody wanted to see these ten coffins, and the funeral rights had to be conducted for each individual person killed, so the funeral lasted a long time. And this was one of the most difficult moments in my entire life, and I can never forget that scene. The people were in a terrible state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court -- this event, what effects did this incident have on the two ethnic groups who had lived for centuries there, the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was terrible, and this had a terrible effect on their good neighbourly relations and their trust in each other. People began to turn their heads away from each other, and they no longer said hello to one another when they met in the streets. We tried to mitigate the situation and say this was one incident that would not repeat itself, and sometimes they thought that we wanted this not to happen in our villages, but they even made fun of us in -- we tried to calm the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you try to go to Dusina to see what had happened in that village? Did the leadership of the HDZ -- you were just an administrative clerk there, but your leaders, the responsible individuals, did they endeavour to have the representatives of the Croatian people go to Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. From the very first day we established contact with the executive authorities of Zenica municipality, with the MUP, with the town mayor, and the president of the HVO who was deputy mayor, and we wanted to take advantage of these people to reach Dusina, and to see on site what had happened and what we could do to overcome this situation so that people would regain confidence and be able to live together again. We wanted to set an example by going there, talking to the Muslims to see what they thought about it. However, this joint visit never occurred. No real reasons were given to us why. An excuse was always found to avoid us going on site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But 30 days after that event, due to force of circumstance, you did go there after all. Could you tell the Court how this happened and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found a way of getting there. I learnt that Dominik Sarkic and Josip, a HVO soldier, would go there with their people, with the president of the assembly and the executive counsel, but we went there ahead of them, and we managed to pass through the checkpoint by saying we were journalists, saying that the others would follow, because we wanted to get there before them. We left the car in an orchard, and we went there and took pictures for our newspaper, Bojovnik, because we wanted to avoid them seizing our camera and our film from us. We saw a house that had been burnt down altogether, the furniture thrown around, the paintings, the bed clothes, and we tried to immortalise this situation so as to be able to show others what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you saw, did that coincide with the description that was given to you by the frightened inhabitants when they came to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most of what they said was confirmed on the spot. Most of what we saw was exactly as they had described it. However, months had gone by and many things had changed. The linen had been was taken away, many things had been destroyed due to rain and everything. So the picture would have been different, certainly, if you had come a day or two afterwards. But the picture, as it was, was terrible. Not an animal could live there, let alone man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher's assistance for another document? We only have it Croatian, but we'll be using as an exhibit only the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D435.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have before you an edition of the newspaper "Bojovnik" or "Soldier." Will you please look at pages 2 and 3 to see the photographs? Before the officials and representatives of the Muslim authorities, you reached the spot, as a journalist, before them. Are these the photographs that you took 30 days after the crime in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the photographs. There were several others, but they were not good. They didn't come out well. The first photograph on the left, you can see a totally burned-down house and a stable behind it and a shed. This house was totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the picture below that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a house with the windows shattered and the furniture destroyed with hammers. To the right is a family picture, a wedding photograph, because it is customary among our people to take photographs at a wedding and keep it as a memento, and you could find many such photographs in the yard. Then, on the right, also some of the appliances that were broken that they couldn't carry away or that didn't attract them. We shot about ten films but many of them were not successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think? Why was something burned and some other things, that might have been useful, completely destroyed and broken? What was the aim of that? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people themselves drew the conclusion that this was a method of intimidating these people, forcing these people to flee. They asked, "What are you doing to us?" And some people would say, "There are too many of us. Someone has to leave these parts." The people who felt bolder made statements of this kind. Others consoled their neighbours and said, "Come back. We'll continue living nicely." Based on those encouraging tales, some of them tried to come back, but they were threatened by the soldiers who told them not to say that to those neighbours. So many of them did not go back. There were 47 Croatian families living in Dusina. There are no more than five or six now. I didn't go there again. I think that there aren't any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That will bring to the end this part of your testimony. We are tendering only the photographs from this Exhibit 435, not the text, because we have spoken at length about these events so we don't think the text is necessary. Let us go on to another area which the Defence would like you, Witness, to testify to. It is Blaskic's speech seeing off the army to Jajce on the 26th of October, 1992. Tell us, on the 26th of October, 1992, where were the HVO units being dispatched from to go to Jajce? Where was this seeing off taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was in a locality called Draga, three kilometres from Busovaca in the direction of Kiseljak. It was a military reception centre with very few facilities where we would prepare our units for the front in Jajce. The weather was terrible that day, it was pouring all day, and we waited for as many soldiers to gather there until nightfall to send them to Jajce. During the line-up of the soldiers, the first to address them was Lieutenant Colonel Filip Filipovic who briefed them on the situation on the front in Jajce, what our chances were, how they should behave as soldiers, how the soldiers should behave during transportation, and so on. I was there as a technical secretary of the HVO, and whenever shifts of soldiers were leaving, I would take cigarettes, soft drinks, and in other ways try to encourage them. After Mr. Filipovic's speech, Colonel Blaskic made a speech, and I couldn't really forget that speech because I found it so inspirational by its humanness, its goodness, its advice to the soldiers, and I took note in a small notebook of his words, and later on, when I came home, I entered this in greater detail in my diary. So I would like to ask permission, Your Honours, to read a part of that speech made by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you are going to read now is what you copied from your personal diary before coming here to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't copy the whole speech when I left for The Hague but only a part of that speech. So may I read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please read very slowly because the interpreters do not have a copy, nor do we? So please read it very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "There are among you, dear soldiers, those who are not collected and who might react to evil with a tenfold stronger evil without thinking about the innocent. My talk with you today and any other in the future will always be sharply intoned towards those who may be rash in that sense."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We are not here in these uniforms and armed with rifles to attack the unarmed and the captured. I will never allow that. I will always ask you and my associates to respect this human rule."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "And for as long as I live, that is how I will try to influence my subordinates." That is part of the notes I took of that speech in my personal diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please -- you were obviously impressed by this speech and this prompted you to take note of it. But tell the Court, was that speech exceptional in any way when it impressed you so? Did Blaskic stand out from those around him by his approach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the soldiers swallowed up his words and listened to him in complete silence. Indeed, I have listened to many speeches, but this one remained in my memory for a long time, and rarely have I seen such noble aims reflected in a speech. I believe that any soldier who heard that speech can never have forgotten it. I published it in our journals, and it was very well-received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of speeches were usually made when people were going to the front? What kind of speeches were they? Were they usually inflammatory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, some soldiers wanted to hear such speeches that would be inflammatory, that would arouse them and prompt them to take radical steps. So, often they wouldn't react to such speeches. They thought it undermined their combat atmosphere. But indeed in those times, speeches of this kind were necessary to calm down the rash and to lead them to the proper path.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall now go on to another area. You were a retired person. You engaged in some social activities, but you and your wife lived in your home in Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, what happened to you in Zenica starting from the 19th of April, 1993, until your departure from Zenica? Who came to your house on the 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you must have learnt from earlier witness statements, in Zenica, the HVO fell, in the military sense, on the 18th of April, which meant that on the very next day, the 19th, parts of BH army units started various reprisals in our neighbourhoods. I lived 2 kilometres from Zenica in the direction of Travnik and Vitez with my wife, and I didn't think I would have to leave those parts because indeed I had done nothing wrong against anyone. But on the 19th, in a red Fiat, three fighters of the BH army arrived, two of them with long barrels came out and without any greetings said, "We request a passenger car from you." I don't remember what brand they said. "A yellow car. That is your car and you need to hand it over to us." I said, "I never had a driving licence nor could I be able to use it. Anyway, a car is not something small, so look around for it." They started insulting me, cursing my Vlaska mother, my Ustasha mother. However, I wanted to avoid any conflict with them because I thought that once they saw that I didn't have a car, they would leave. But my wife wasn't like me, so she answered back in the same way, she cursed them back. And so this one lost his nerve and said, "I'm from Ahmici." He was about 20. And he cocked his rifle. He hit me with the rifle butt in the chest and he slapped my wife. He said, "I'm going to kill you if, within five minutes, you don't tell us where your weapons are and where your car is." We were ready to die because we couldn't answer that question. And these threats, humiliations, they even forced me to kneel down, people were collecting in the street in front of my house to watch, my wife refused to kneel down. He hit me with a rifle butt, forcing me to kneel. I kept thinking that I could delay things and the worst thing wouldn't happen, that is, they wouldn't kill me. Then his colleague, the one who came with him out of the car, couldn't go on watching this behaviour. He took his rifle away from him. And so the two of them went off because this one was really in a fury and he would have done the worst if this other one hadn't stopped him and had the courage to stop him. He was out of his mind, he was so furious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the first incident on the 19th of April, 1993. However, six days later, on the 25th of April, 1993, again a group of six came to your house. Would you explain to the Court who they were, what they wanted, and what they did to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these were terrible times. Six armed soldiers came in, two with firearms and others with knives and wires for strangling. They were Mujahedeen. I recognised them easily because I saw them for months walking around Zenica. They were wearing green capes, short trousers above the ankles, in tennis shoes, dark-skinned with a kind of cap on their heads and with beards. They couldn't speak our language but they had an interpreter, a student, a metallurgy student whom I knew by sight because he lived in my neighbourhood and he studied metallurgy for ten years in Zenica. He came from Algeria and he served as their interpreter. We would meet in the grocery stop and we would even nod our heads at each other to say hello. But we didn't know each other personally. So he came to my house and he was their interpreter. One of these who led this group asked me to go to a room with him and to be there alone with him, and he asked me, "Do you have a weapon? If you do, tell us, and we will go quickly." I said, "I have nothing to give you. I have nothing to say to you. I never had any weapons, especially not a machine gun or a radio transmitter." Then he looked around the room, took down a picture, and told me to trample on it, that is a crucifixion and he told me to trample on it. He couldn't speak, but he showed what he wanted me to do with his hands. Then he looked through my books, and he -- a 500 mark note fell out of the book. He told me to keep quiet about it, he took it from me, and then again he showed me that if they find any weapons on me, I would have had it. They broke everything in the apartment. They forced me to turn the beds over, the furniture. They looked through everything. There was a neighbour visiting and my wife. They forced her -- them to stand against the wall. They told me that I mustn't leave the house without their permission, and they stayed there for about two hours. That was my first encounter with the Mujahedeen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you understand this, "that you mustn't leave the house without letting us know"? What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, I couldn't understand why I was so important to them that I shouldn't leave the house. However, five days after this visit, 30 soldiers appeared. There were not just Mujahedeen but with them were members of the BH army of the 33rd and other brigades and of the Military Police, 30 soldiers in all, they surrounded my house, and with pointed long barrels they entered the house and said, "You're having a meeting." I said, "What kind of meeting?" And they said, "We have a report that people from Vitez are coming to a meeting." I couldn't understand. They went around the house firing. Later on, my impression was that Croats were living around my house and that this whole scene was staged to force them to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please slow down a little. I understand you get rather excited and then you start speaking more quickly, but you are making the interpreters' task very difficult, to interpret perfectly correctly what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. It is 11.00. We will take a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us resume. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DL, we stopped at the point when 30 soldiers burst into your house. What did they ask for? What were they looking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, they had received some kind of information that a meeting would be held at my place with people from Busovaca and Vitez. So they got into the house, they searched the basement and the attic, and they realised that no one was there, and then they took me into detention. A white Kombi van stood in the yard, there were two soldiers there, and he took me towards the Kombi and said, "You're coming with us." I didn't even manage to get dressed. I was wearing my slippers, the ones that I wear at home, and I said, "I have to put on some proper shoes and I have to get dressed." My wife said, "He has blood pressure and he needs medicine." This other guy said, "No, he doesn't need any medicine. He's coming with us and that's it." They brought me to this vehicle, and then, as I got to the vehicle, I was hoping that they'd take me to this specified place, this prison. But all of a sudden, they changed their minds. Two of them said, "Listen, you go back. Our assignment is to keep you in house custody, so you are not allowed to leave your home, you cannot leave town, and you cannot leave your home without our approval and our permission." So I remained in custody at home. Even my next-door neighbours were not allowed to communicate with me at all and they didn't even dare say hello to me, they were so frightened, and some of them said that, "Well, why don't they take you away and let's get this over with" because they were fed up with having the military in my yard all the time and this embarrassing situation every now and then. This really bothered them. I took all kinds of measures in order to have an exchange carried out so that I could leave that area because I saw that if I stayed on there, that some night, they will come, as they did come later on, after night. I didn't dare sleep in the night at home, I would just leave the lights on, and my wife and I would escape from my home. We didn't dare spend the night at the house because there were so many uncontrolled units, the police could not control all of them, and they could have done whatever they wanted to do, as they did in some places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, because we don't really have to describe every single incident, in addition to these three described incidents, how many times did groups of soldiers, armed soldiers, burst into your house in addition to these three times that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I didn't keep records, but my wife managed to, and she said that twelve times, twelve times, armed soldiers got into our house, twelve times. And they came individually. For example, they would come to my balcony, and one of them brought a Croatian flag and made me walk over it, and he did too. This was a great pleasure for him. He always carried this Croatian flag, and whenever he'd come to my house, he'd make me walk over and he'd walk over it. But, you know, they weren't as terrible as the first three were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a total of twelve times that soldiers burst into your house. What was your understanding of the situation? Could you stay on there, or was all of this done for the reason of your leaving Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finally realised that I no longer belonged there, that my life was in danger, my wife's life was in danger, and also my next-of-kin too, and nobody dared come to my place. I asked the official authorities, the Red Cross, and they had some kind of an institution through which they arranged for exchanges, and I asked them -- and they were stationed at the stadium, the sports stadium -- and I said that I wanted to get exchanged, to go anywhere, and I simply couldn't take it anymore, it was nerve-racking, and I was not capable of thinking anymore and I thought all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when were you exchanged? On what date and where did you go, in which direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day, there was a pleasant surprise in store for me. A Bosniak woman came with her family, and she said that she was sent from this centre of exchange and she said that she got my house and that I was supposed to be exchanged. I was pleased. I felt that it was salvation. I just took my clothes, the basic necessities, my wife and I, and we went to a small Kombi van and we were exchanged. This was on the 23rd of November, 1993. I went in the direction of Zepce, that is where the exchange was carried out, and at that time I was under HVO-controlled territory. So this was my salvation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your wife took just one suitcase; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one suitcase. They didn't allow us to take anything else. We could only take the things that we had on ourselves. I took a sweater, a coat, an overcoat, and my wife too, because we didn't know how far we would travel and we didn't know where this would end and how far we would have to go on foot and we didn't know whether we could manage to carry everything, so we just took the very, very basic stuff. We left all sorts of things. We left furniture, food. It was full. The house was full of different things, and all of it just stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were saved. What about your house today? Did you eventually return to your house in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim family came in before I left, and they stayed in my house until 1996, and as they were leaving, as they went back to their place of residence in Zepce, they emptied my house. Well, okay, let it be. But another thing was that they destroyed it, the floor, the windows. They cut out all the electricity, the waterworks. They broke my bathtub, my boiler, electric boiler. A neighbour of mine called me and said, "Take a look at your house. It's all empty." I saw it and it looked like nothing you have ever seen. That is the way things have been until the present day. I asked the municipal authorities to allow me to come back, and I would like to get hold of some money in order to get it built up again because I would like to return to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have concluded our questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Now it is the Office of the Prosecutor that will have some questions for you. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, and counsel, good morning. Good morning, Witness DL.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My name is Mark Harmon, Witness DL. I am one of the Prosecutors on this case, and my colleagues to my right, Mr. Gregory Kehoe and Mr. Andrew Cayley are assisting me. I only intend to ask you a few questions about your testimony this morning, but let me, if I could, Mr. President, first of all, go into private session because I would like to ask Witness DL some questions that were raised in the private session on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could we have a private session now? (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DL, let me focus your attention on the crimes that took place in the village of Dusina for just a moment. I take it from your testimony that you were not there when those terrible crimes occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your testimony you mentioned that contact was made with the ABiH after you and your colleagues became aware of those crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not with the BH army. No contact was established with them. But with the Ministry of the Interior, the police from Zenica, so that they would make sure that the BH army would allow us to pass checkpoints so that we would come and see whether everything the people told us in our statements was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you personally contact representatives of the Minister of the Interior in respect of the crimes at Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I did not hold such a high post. I couldn't have done it. This was done by the President of the municipal committee of HDZ, Mr. Pojvnik Josip, and Mr. Sakic Dominik. They were the ones who were authorised, and they were the ones who had the authority to negotiate. I was a technical secretary. I organised meetings for them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your testimony was that members of the ABiH, the Armija, were responsible for the crimes that took place at Dusina. Were the particular units that were involved identified to you by the survivors and the refugees from Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we asked them whether they knew any one of those soldiers whom they had seen, whether they were their neighbours or something, they said that they did not know those people, that it was no one from the neighbourhood who was in uniform. But later we heard from Mr. Dzidic, who was the political representative of the Bosniak people, he was some kind of a spokesman of the SDA, when contact was established with them -- with him, he said that an investigation would be carried out against these persons, and he asserted that it wasn't that this was some kind of organised activity by the BH army, but that this was just done at random. However, that was not true. Later it was ascertained that these people had uniforms, they had weapons. They belonged to some of the units of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Witness DL, is: Do you know which units those people belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. None of us could find anything out from these statements that we got from these people. And later, during the investigation, I don't know whether something was established. So I could not ascertain which units these soldiers belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness DL, whether an investigation was ever contacted by the Muslim authorities into the events of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if there was a failure to investigate the crimes at Dusina and to immediately investigate those crimes, was that, in your opinion, a grievous error?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. We had assumed, like any normal person would have, that investigating this crime would be a warning to other villages to take care, to prevent such terrible situations from happening, and to report this to the regular police, et cetera. And we thought that such proceedings would be very helpful in terms of preventing such things from happening again. However, this, indeed, never took place, because we never heard that somebody was detained, or punished, or that investigative proceedings were initiated. We were really sorry. And we realised that the media didn't even write about it, so the citizens of Zenica were not informed about this incident at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness DL, you testified that the acts that occurred in Dusina were acts of terror, and it was a method by which Croats were forced to leave their village. Do you remember your testimony in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the events that took place in the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is beyond the direct-examination. Ahmici was not within the scope of the direct-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. Mr. Harmon, please try to remain within the scope of the direct-examination, because Mr. Nobilo is right, or perhaps you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware of any similar type of acts that occurred in respect of the Muslim civilian population in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no. I had heard nothing, up until what had happened in Dusina and the downfall of the HVO in Zenica. I did not hear of anything similar taking place in the vicinity. I didn't perform such a function. My duties were not that kind, and the information that did reach me was not very serious information, they were more rumours, or guesswork or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Subsequent to the events in Dusina, in other words, after the 26th of January, 1993, up until the end of 1993, did you hear of any events directed against the Muslim population where Muslim civilians were killed, Muslim houses were burned, and Muslim civilians were forced to flee their villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, once again this is beyond the scope of the investigation-in-chief (sic). We only asked the witness about events in January in Dusina, nothing after that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, the microphone was not switched on. The President said that he saw no reason why the Prosecutor could not ask the witness whether he heard of any similar events after January, 1993. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask whether it is correct that at one stage the evidence was that one man, presumably an assailant, said that he was from Ahmici, or perhaps I misheard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that young man who was -- he had the rifle, he hit me, and he said, "I'll show you what a young man from Ahmici means and can do. I am from Ahmici." That is what he said. He was the angriest of them all. And I had never heard of the village beforehand. I had never heard of that village. I had no need to. And he said, "I'm going to show you who I am, and what I am, and what I can do and you're going to sing a nice little song after that." And he expressly said he was from Ahmici. I could not have concluded that he was from Ahmici. I did not know where Ahmici was, what place it was. I didn't even know all our surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like the translation to be done. We did limit the questions on Ahmici, but I do not think it is a illegitimate or unfair for Mr. Harmon to ask the witness, as a member of the HDZ, when knew of other events that took place after the crimes committed in Dusina. So, please, put your question, Mr. Harmon, in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DL, after the crimes in Dusina that occurred on the 26th of January, 1993, did you hear of any crimes perpetrated by the HVO and directed against Muslim civilians, including the murder, the intentional burning of their houses and the forced expulsion of Muslim civilians? Did you hear of any of those types of crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't hear of them. I didn't read the papers. I didn't follow radio programmes. I was -- I had had enough of even the things that I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DL, let me turn your attention to another subject, and that is you testified that you were present at a situation when troops, HVO troops, in Busovaca were being sent off to the front at Jajce. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you oftentimes go to Draga where the troops were collected and sent off to the front at Jajce, or were you there only on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the last group of troops to go. I went once, the first time when our unit went. I was in charge of supplying beverages and cigarettes for these troops. Everybody had to have one packet of cigarettes per day while he was doing this duty. So if it was seven days, he would have to be given seven packets of cigarettes. So those were my functions. That's what I did, and that was that particular instance. The last time, on the 26th of October, 1992, when Colonel Blaskic made his speech, I was there then. I remained there one to one and half hours and then returned to Zenica after that. I didn't have a uniform. I was a civilian. I didn't have any other tasks, any other duties, just on the part of the civilian section of the HVO to give the soldiers their beverages, and their cigarettes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DL, other than this one occasion on the 26th of October, 1992, did you ever go to any other assembly of troops, HVO troops, where the soldiers were addressed either by then Colonel Blaskic or addressed by any other HVO military leader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go any more. I went on the two occasions that I stated, and I was happy to have seen our soldiers gathered together. It wasn't a real army, they were volunteers. On some occasions there were 50 of them from our unit, sometimes 30. So people were not duty-bound to go there, and there were always a different number of people. The further things progressed, the fewer soldiers there were. I don't know the reason for this, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness DL, you mentioned two occasions. One occasion I'm aware of, the 26th of October, 1992. When was the other occasion you were present when soldiers were assembled and being sent to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the first time, on the 15th of August, 1992, and General Blaskic wasn't there to see them off on that occasion. I, once again, took them cigarettes and soft drinks, and that was on the 15th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Colonel Blaskic address his troops at a time when the HVO was engaged in combat with the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I could not have. I was not a military man. I couldn't even approach let alone hear any of his speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, Witness DL, you said that -- and correct me if I'm wrong, that some of the leaders of the HVO military made rash speeches to the soldiers who were assembled and who were going to be sent to the front-lines against the Serbs. Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said -- what I said was this: First of all, on the 26th of October, Lieutenant-Colonel Filipovic took the floor first, and it was his duty to take all these groups up to the front-line and to return the group of soldiers there, to return them back. So he was in charge of the safety of the units going and coming. And he discussed conduct. He said how they should behave, that they were not to turn the lights on in vehicles, that they were to make a lot of noise, so he gave them technical instructions. And he did not speak about morale or anything of that kind, he just spoke about the technical conduct and the way they should behave going and coming from the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did any HVO military officer, in your presence, make any kind of a speech that you thought was unnecessary or unprofessional?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. While I was present, no. I can't say. No. But whether there were -- there was anything of that kind elsewhere or at other times, I don't know. I was not -- did not have any military duties, as I said, and I didn't have the opportunity of coming by knowledge of this kind, information of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the occasion when you described the speech by then Colonel Blaskic, was that the only occasion when you had to meet Colonel Blaskic, or did you meet him on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have occasion to meet him, but I was present when our unit took their oath. He made a short speech there, along the same lines. I was not involved. That is to say, I didn't make a note of that speech. It was a short speech because there were many speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did it appear to you, Witness DL, that the soldiers under Colonel Blaskic's command respected him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: During the ceremonies, such as oath-taking ceremony and so on, everything was at a high cultural level, so they showed respect towards Colonel Blaskic. But I don't want to enter into the individual opinions of him, of any commander or him. Whether he -- they liked him or not, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me clarify one part of your testimony, and that relates to the terrible events that occurred to you on April 19th in Zenica, when three soldiers appeared at your house. One of them, you said, was in a fury, he was out of his mind, and he struck you with a rifle butt and he slapped you. Was that the soldier who said he was from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The other soldier standing behind him, he wasn't -- he didn't want to behave in that way. I didn't notice the fury of the first young man, because the first young man was really furious and irritated. First of all, because he said to me, "Look at the car I'm driving. I'm driving a small Fiat and you've hidden your car somewhere. You have weapons, you have this, you have that, whereas I don't." And I was not able to communicate with the young man because he took every -- each of my words amiss, and anything I said he would spit at me, he would spit in my face, spit at my chest. When he spat at my wife, she spat back at him. He was really out of his mind with fury. He said, "If you don't tell me where our car is, I'm going to cut you down immediately." He was far more furious and active in his investigation than the other man. The other man couldn't take much of this. In fact, he left. He took his rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DL, do you have any idea why that man from Ahmici was so furious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no idea. He was a young man. And I (sic) said, "I'll show you what a man from Ahmici can do." And in that first instance I didn't make head or tail of this. I didn't know what he wanted to say by that, what he meant by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I have just a moment? Witness DL, Thank you very much. I have no further questions. That concludes my cross-examination, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you wish to exercise your right to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, with only two questions. Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness DL, when this young man barged into your house saying he was from Ahmici, and you couldn't understand his fury because you hadn't heard of Ahmici while you were in Zenica, but tell the Court later on, '94, '95, '96, '97, until the present moment, did you later learn that an HV (sic) unit came to Ahmici, set the village on fire and killed the civilians? So just that there should be no misunderstanding, there is an error in the transcript, it is an "HVO" unit, not an "HV" unit. Therefore, my question is: Did you hear of any such event later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear later on that this had happened in Ahmici, that -- in a village near Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the units were being lined up, that is the Jure Francetic Brigade from Zenica, how many people spoke on that occasion, if you can remember, in addition to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four or five speakers, including Zivko Totic. They were all addressing the soldiers. They greeted them and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 1st of August, 1992, when you attended for the first time ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of August, when the troops were being seen off to Jajce, who spoke then? Were there several speakers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite -- there was quite a large number of soldiers at the time. There were about 80 of them. And again, Mr. Filipovic addressed them and the commanders of the units from Kakanj, Zenica, Vitez, each one of them addressed the soldiers. These speeches mainly related to the behaviour. We didn't have much experience at the time, so that somebody could give more high-quality information regarding the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you compare all those speeches on the 15th of August and the line-up of the Jure Francetic unit, did Blaskic's speech stand apart? Was it different in some way? Was it distinct from all the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly enjoy hearing a kind word. I like to read a lot, and this speech really moved me, and I couldn't forget it. It was imprinted in my memory, and I shall always remember it gladly. Even the most primitive soldier, if he had never heard what one should not do in contact with civilians when one is armed, or with a captured soldier, that I'm sure he would have learned from that speech something that he will remember for his life. And from that speech I saw him as a commander who really wanted a fair and honest battle to be fought if it does occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Now the Judges will have a few questions for you, Witness DL, and then your testimony will be over. I first turn to Judge Riad. Please proceed, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness DL, I'm going to call you DL. Good day to you. I have a single question to put to you concerning the influence of General Blaskic over his soldiers. It is more the psychological side of things, because you told us how moved you were by this speech made by General Blaskic, that it touched you, that his speech generally reflected some noble goals which, as you've just said, could affect the most primitive soldiers. What did this speech consist of? Was it the sole speech that you heard, the one and only speech that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion I also heard Mr. Filipovic's speech, which is more of a technical nature, who said how soldiers should behave on the front, how they should show courage, how they should dig in, how they should camouflage themselves. However, this speech differed drastically from that one. It was more of giving advice. It was a speech in which he said what an HVO soldier should do in -- when he comes in contact with the population, with civilians, with captured soldiers, prisoners of war. Mr. Blaskic said it was not up to us to settle accounts with civilians. Every soldier should protect them and take them to security if there are any hostilities in their village. So I don't know how all the soldiers were affected by this speech, but I hope that it was received in a positive sense, and that they took note of it, and that they acted accordingly. At least that is my hope, that it had the same impression on them as it did on me. A positive one, therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In any event, you said that it could affect even the most primitive soldiers and that it had a good influence and that he spoke in a very noble tone, with humanity, in fact, that one should act against any war crimes. But after the 26th of October, 1992, you did not learn of him using, shall I call it, this influence, this good influence that he had over soldiers, to address them again in the months that followed in the course of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not have the privilege of hearing him again. The battles in Jajce were over because Jajce fell on the 30th of October, 1992, and our units were transferred to other fronts, to Turbe and to Travnik, so I did not have the privilege of hearing General Blaskic again, and I can tell you, Your Honours, that I'm sorry to have missed them if there were any. I didn't have the opportunity to hear him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were involved in the media. You said that you were a journalist at times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't a journalist, I was a member of the board of editors of our journal. I was assigned to provide funds for printing this journal, for the paper required, for the printing. I had to look for a donator for every single issue, a sponsor. So that was my duty. That was my duty as a member of the board of editors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness DL, could you look again at two documents, D433A and D434A? Shall we look first at D434 because it is prior in time; it is dated 27th January whereas D433 is dated 20th January. Would I be right, sir, would I be right in thinking that both documents were addressed to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command and that, accordingly, they were intended to reach Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, they should have reached Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, crimes were committed at Dusina, and you said the people who committed the crimes were ABiH soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: At that time, the ABiH was collaborating with the HVO in resisting the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did any reports reach you as to whether these ABiH soldiers who committed these crimes gave any explanation as to why they were acting in the way they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately, we didn't get any such feedback information, though we craved for it. We wanted to know the real identity of those units, the identity of those men. If they were men from the outside, that we should jointly take measures against them. That is what our officials thought. So that no such thing should happen again, no such incident. Unfortunately, we did not manage to learn the names of the units nor of the individuals. We tried in every possible way to find out, but we didn't succeed. Perhaps high-level organs did learn something, but we were never told. At least I personally never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you take the view that having regard to the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH, that what happened was strange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was strange because our soldiers at the Jajce front were right next to the Muslim units, units from Jajce who were Bosniaks. So it was astonishing to us. We had lost faith, and it is very difficult to restore trust on both sides. So we tried again. The leaders of my party and the leaders of the SDA party, after those events, organised joint public meetings in local communities, in Lokvine, Gornja Zenica, Klug, Crkvica, and the television broadcast these meetings, the aim being to avoid a repetition of such incidents. And, of course, questions were asked, because these meetings were held in public, representatives of the HVO and the HDZ and representatives of the BH army, they tried to reduce tension, but to what extent they succeeded, the best evidence is what happened on the 18th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to Zvonko Rajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I apologise to me for my very execrable pronunciation. How was he killed, did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The local people who first reached us said that when they looked for Zvonko Rajic and he surrendered, they took him together with a friend of his behind the house and shot him. The shots were heard, so they concluded that Zvonko was indeed killed with firearms, and that is what they reported to us that same day when they came to the Croatian centre, that Zvonko was executed behind his house. Then they went on to list the names of others who were killed, in their opinion, and we took those names down. But our report of that day and this one differs both in terms of the number of killed and the number of wounded because they couldn't be identical. The same people were not writing those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. I see. You recognise there is a difference between the written report and your own report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, look at 434, midway. Midway, you will see a line that says: "Zvonko Rajic, son of Ivo, was killed during the negotiations." How do you react to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of negotiations they're referring to when a person was killed within five minutes.
