The eyewitnesses told us they just took him behind the house and, as soon as they got hold of him, they liquidated him immediately. There was no investigation. There was no need for any explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next page of that document, page 2 of that same document, you remember some of the MOS people wanted to shoot Zdravka Rados. She was the wife of Dragan Rados.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And the line goes on to say: "It is assumed that they abandoned their idea to carry out the execution at the request of a local Muslim." Were there other local Muslims who thought that what happened was wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes, and we were pleased that it was so, and there were people who tried to help in a way, but to tell you the truth, very quickly such people were silenced. In my own personal case, you know, there was a doctor who went to school with me, to

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: not to because I live in town and there is something unpleasant that might happen to me," and there were others who tried to help me; and I'm sure that there were good people who offer their homes, to put up others, but they couldn't go on doing that for very long because it wasn't all that easy for them either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, later on, you personally experienced some unpleasantness. The houses around you were Croat houses or Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, speaking geometrically, if we look at the radius, there were houses belonging to Croats all around and the Bosniak houses were far away. There were new neighbours of mine and old neighbours of mine. My old Bosniak neighbours were not as radical towards me and my family in comparison to those who came later and who didn't know me because I always used to resolve common problems together with them in the local community, like when we first got telephones, electricity, et cetera. So we had a very good relationship. But those people who didn't know me well enough behaved differently, those who were not aware of my good intentions. A soldier who came to me said, "Your next-door neighbours, you know, the ones living up there, they follow what you do everyday and they report to me, you know?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You remember you told us that some of your neighbours said to you, "Come back. We will continue to live nicely," or words to that effect. Who were those neighbours, Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was leaving, my neighbours -- my neighbours were in tears. They were afraid that it would be their turn now to experience what I had

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: what about us? You are leaving and we're staying behind." A Muslim there, who was a driver, I talked to him and I wanted to have some money, you know, when -- before I left, and I asked him if he wanted to buy some roof tiles from me, and I said, "Do you want to buy this so that we can have some money on us," you know? And he said, "Why would I have to pay you for this because I'm going to take it for free. I'm going to take it when I need it. Why would I pay you for it?" These people simply didn't dare come up to me. When they saw how many times the police came to my place, they didn't dare come. The other day, I went to my place, and a Bosniak, an old family friend, came. He hugged me, he kissed me, and he said that he was pleased to see that I was alive, and he said, "Please come back." He said that several times he and his son wanted to protect me but they didn't dare. They were afraid for their families. That's what he told me only the other day, that he did wish to help me but that he didn't have the courage to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did some people say to you that if you remain we would continue to "live nice," or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, there weren't conditions for that at that time and one could not harbour such illusions. People were afraid. They wished me a safe journey and they said that they hoped that this would be over soon, and until the present day, they've been asking me when I will come back. Some do want to see me back there but others -- well, you know, time will show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I misheard you on that point. Now, do you judge, Witness DL, that relations between the two communities will mend eventually, that there will be a healing of relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm speaking from my experience. I'm 60 years old, and I've experienced so many things, but I think that when the economic problems of my town are solved and when more people get jobs and when the education system is put in place again, when there are no differences in that respect, that these things will be overcome and forgotten soon. Of course, major crimes cannot be forgotten all that easily. But, you know, people will struggle to survive and to live normally, and they will have to fit into a normal life and they will have to find a common tongue. On my own part, I'm in charge of a rugby club, precisely with that intention in mind, because I want to have this overcome in the sports field. So we hope that through sports and things like that, we are going to establish contacts, and in this way, we're going to overcome the current situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My recollection is that you said that there were about 47 Croat families in your area and that now there are only five or six left. Is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Those Croat families, did they continue to live there throughout this troubled period, or did they go in and come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're talking about Dusina, Dusina. Yes. Forty-six, that is what they said, 46 families. These five or six, up to eleven, they were quite persistent and they probably had a different attitude towards their property and they didn't want to leave it behind altogether, so they would come out and come back. But they had to pass through various checkpoints. They say whenever they passed these checkpoints, they were searched, and others were not. Others could carry whatever they wanted to into the village and they could carry anything they wanted to out of the village, but these people, no, they had to be searched. Obviously these people were afraid that some kind of explosive devices would be brought in or -- explosives or whatever. So they didn't really live there. They were actually staying in town and coming to see their properties and going back. I don't know whether they renewed their houses, not yet, I think, but I believe that that will take place some day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you remember when you were hit with a rifle butt, another ABiH soldier took away the rifle from the soldier who had hit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did your reports suggest to you that amongst the ABiH there were other soldiers of the same kind of disposition as the soldier who took away that rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, I came to the conclusion that there were some who were truly human. These younger men sometimes were punished by others if they did not do the things they were asked to do, and I really admire this young man, and if I were to see him some place, I would like to thank him and congratulate him on having done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand. So let me ask you a last question. It arises from document D433. The second paragraph says that "the Muslim authorities were denying access without the presence of the EC monitors." Will you look at that for me, the second paragraph? I think this is talking about Dusina. The whole sentence reads: "However, the monitors failed to arrive at the arranged time, and therefore the identification has not yet been carried out because the Muslim authorities are denying access without the presence of the EC monitors." Did you have any impression as to why the Muslim authorities wanted the EC monitors to be present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go in depth, as far as this problem is concerned, but I imagine they wanted to get rid of the problem altogether so that somebody else would do the things that they were supposed to do because they had a hospital nearby, they had experts, professionals. They simply wanted to get rid of this burden, they wanted somebody else to shoulder it, and that is why this went so slowly and that is why they didn't go to the spot. They kept waiting. Obviously, they didn't want this meeting to take place. I wasn't really familiar with all of this and -- what was the name? It wasn't SFOR. It was UNPROFOR, yes. I wasn't very familiar with them. So I imagine that that was the reason, to perhaps have somebody else cover up for their irresponsibility or their lack of knowledge so that somebody else could do the identification wrong or whatever. That was the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You don't suppose that they wanted an impartial person to be around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That might be the case too, yes. It might be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you my last, last question. It is about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- the speech made by Colonel Blaskic. As you described it, it was indeed a lofty speech, something that one may compare, for example, with the kind of speech that I imagine a Roman centurion would give to his soldiers as compared with the speech that an inspired General would give. You said you published that speech in your newspaper? Did you publish the speech in your journal or newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first wrote it down in my personal diary because -- it was in Zenica because I was at home, so I was so profoundly impressed that I had to write it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I asked if you published it in your newspaper or in your journals. You did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. In the newspaper Branimir, which is a newspaper published by the Association of Retired Veterans of the War, so I wanted all soldiers, because all soldiers and all units do get it, I wanted them all to read about this, and this article of mine really resounded throughout the ranks and I was commended for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you bring a copy of your newspaper with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't. I have a copy at home, but I had assumed that I gave Mr. Nobilo a copy. I don't know. Maybe I thought I did and then just forgot about it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DL, I have two first and two last questions for you, and please don't hold me to my word, I ask the interpreters. I would like to know the place where the HVO troops were gathering, assembling, the place where General Blaskic made this speech which inspired you so and moved you so. Was it an HVO camp, this assembly point, Draga, I think you called it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Soldiers would gather there only from time to time because there wasn't really enough space for soldiers to live there, to stay there. There was a restaurant and there was a small building and there was a big concrete plateau where there would be a review of all the soldiers and then they would simply leave. It was closest to Busovaca, Zenica, Vitez, Kakanj, so people who could manage to come, they would. But sometimes half of the unit would come and the other half wouldn't come because all of this was on a voluntary basis so nobody was held responsible if they didn't come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Was it a camp for the training of soldiers? Some kind of training for soldiers, was it provided there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. This was during the days of the former Yugoslavia, something that was used by the former air force. It was a radar station. I think you can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So in the environs, were there any training camps for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was there twice. I don't know. Perhaps somewhere in some of the surrounding places. I have no idea whether they did have some kind of exercise grounds or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As far as I understood, were there one or several camps where the HVO was trained? It is a very simple question. Do you know or do you not know? because it seemed to me, as a member of the HVO, you would know whether there were places where the HVO troops were trained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know what? Just like any army, I saw a few times that they were practising some things with the soldiers, you know, how to march, how to handle a rifle or whatever. But I wasn't present there. I didn't know whether they had any kind of tactical exercises, whether they had exercises grounds or whatever for training soldiers. I'm not aware of that, at least as far as Zenica is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And my last, last, last question: You have told us repeatedly how impressed you were by the speech of the accused, and thanks to the questions put to you by my colleague Judge Shahabuddeen, I hope that we will have a copy of that speech which appears to be remarkable. So I'm interested regarding the other speeches. You said that they were unreasonable. Do you remember you said that? That compared to the other speeches which were unreasonable and inflammatory, Blaskic's speech stood out. In what respect were those other speeches unreasonable? Did they shock you? Did they speak of patriotism and nationalism to such an extent that it shocked you? Could you tell us that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Very often these speeches were made by commanders who were not up to it, who were not up to command posts, and their speeches were uninspiring, nothing to write home about, nothing worth recording or remembering, and I really thought they were uneducated. Nothing special. But this one really stood out, so I automatically forgot all the others. I didn't want to remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not talking to you about the form of those speeches, but you said that they were speeches that were not reasonable and even inflammatory, I think you said. So I want to know, when you describe those speeches as inflammatory and not being reasonable, they were made by HVO commanders, so try and remember because you were obviously impressed by the speech of the accused and, on the other hand, there were these inflammatory speeches. What did they say in those inflammatory speeches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, when a commander speaks to his soldiers and is not familiar with the situation on the ground and the battlefield, and he says that, "Anything is possible, you should just do this, you should just do that, you just need this, you just need that, we are strong, we are organised," but that was not true at all. You know, that kind of speech. And even the soldiers were a bit suspicious about this, because not all the soldiers were educated to the same level, and others were aware of the situation, others were not. So it was just words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, let me ask my question very directly: Were they anti-Serb speeches, anti-Muslim speeches or simply Croat speeches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were speeches addressed at the enemy, rather, "The enemy is this, the enemy is that. We are such and such, and the enemy is such and such," in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And who was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who was the enemy? The Serb enemy. For a long time it was the Serb army. They were our enemy for a long time at Jajce, at Zepce, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DL, I'm talking to you about this meeting on, I think, the 20th of October, about this rally on that date. The speeches of those commanders that you described as inflammatory, were they speeches addressed against the Serbs, against the Muslims, against whom? Try and remember, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the 26th of October. This was the last stage of fighting against -- at Jajce. It was Colonel Filipovic who spoke about technical things. He told the soldiers what the dangers were of going to Jajce and coming back, because there were Serb units that could jeopardise them. He explained how one should behave at the front-line, that one should not drink alcoholic beverages, that there should be no indecent behaviour. That's what he spoke of. He was quite definite, quite specific. I remember his speech. These others, who were addressing their soldiers, they were very unprofessional speeches. They all addressed their units, and they said that they should be courageous soldiers, brave soldiers, that they should all be proud of them. So these speeches were not really worth remembering or writing about them in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I think it is over for you now. And even though we had quite a number of questions for you, the Tribunal has not, believe us, forgotten the suffering you went through. The Tribunal is simply trying to hear the various sides of the story to establish the truth, but we are aware of your suffering, and we thank you for coming as far as The Hague to testify. So it is over for you. Please do the not move for the moment. We are going to adjourn for about 20 minutes, and we will resume at 1.00 for a final half hour. You do have another witness, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The meeting is adjourned until 1.00. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we go on to the next witness we should like to tender the exhibits into evidence. The exhibits presented through the previous witness, that is the map, and Exhibits D434 and 435 -- 433, 434 and 435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objections? Thank you. Can we please wait for a few moments until the witness is brought in? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, sir? Please remain standing for a minute. Will you tell us your name, family name, first name, your age, your profession, and your place of residence now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mladen Holman, son of Karlo. My mother's name is Slavica. Name Udiljak. I was born in Doboj in 1958. I completed my education in Zenica, the high school for coaches in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you reside now or do you prefer not to tell us that? And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do wish to say that I am now living in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And what is your occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a coach of karate. I have a diploma of the school that I completed in Sarajevo, attached to the Physical Education Faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is simply to identify you for the benefit of the Judges. Remain standing for a moment to make your solemn declaration, which the usher is going to hand to you, so please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated now, Mr. Holman. Please answer the questions of Mr. Nobilo, who, together with Mr. Hayman, have called you to appear as a witness in the case against General Blaskic. We'll be adjourning quite shortly, but we will resume work in a week's time. Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Holman, would you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born and what schools you graduated from, and what you were doing in Zenica before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: I was born in Doboj, as I said, in 1958. My mother's name is Slavica, nee Udiljak, and father Karlo. I am married, I have three children. I completed elementary and secondary school in Zenica. The coach school in Sarajevo where I received a diploma as a sports coach.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please speak more slowly, because I too speak more quickly outside the courtroom, but in the courtroom let us try and speak slowly so that the interpreters can accurately convey your words. So prior to the war, you were involved in sports. You were a coach in a karate club; weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you joined any military unit and how this happened. Explain this to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in 1991, in October and November, HOS units were established. That is the Croatian Defence Forces. Mr. Matija Brajnovic, who was a coordinator of the Croatian Party of Rights for Bosnia, talking to me, told me about this and asked me whether I wanted to join in the defence against aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, when you were asked to join these HOS units, who was the aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: The aggressor was the Serbian side. I still had some qualms, but I decided definitely to join those units when I saw, on television, the suffering of Vukovar. I remember well that this happened on the 20th of November. My people were being victimised, and I want to assist my people as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And so you joined the HOS unit. Did you go alone or did you bring some young men with you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: In the time while I was thinking this over, I talked about it with my friends and my sporting friends, because I thought such men would be very welcome in defence, capable men, and my conclusion was that I could join, together with some 30 people. So I went on the 12th of November to the cultural centre Napredak where a meeting was underway, and I reported that I had a platoon strong unit and that I could join. The chief of the staff for HOS -- of HOS for Bosnia was Jadranko Jandric. Am I speaking too quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: The chief of HOS for Bosnia was Jadranko Jandric. There was a separate chief for Bosnia his name was Blaz Kraljevic. I mention that -- him, that his name was Blaz, because I will be mentioning another Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you went to the Croatian Cultural Society in Napredak to join the HOS. Who gave you the uniforms and the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: The first uniforms and the first weapons were given to us by Mr. Dobroslav Paraga from Zagreb and Mr. Brajnovic coordinated these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Mr. Dobroslav Paraga was president?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: President of the Croatian Party of Rights and the commander of HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So when you joined, together with 30 men, what position were you appointed to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: I was appointed to commander of a platoon. Later on, within a month or so, I advanced to company commander, and then battalion commander, and later on I became Deputy Chief of Staff of the command for HOS for Bosnia, Jadranko Jandric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you were promoted from platoon commander, that is a platoon of 30 men, to Deputy Chief of Staff of the command for the whole of Bosnia? How many months did this take?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: About two months. That is, until the new year. So from October until January. Within 10 or 12 months I achieved such a promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you be more specific with regard to the year? October which year? 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, please, tell us, in 1991, in October, you joined the HOS and became platoon commander. And when did you become Deputy Chief of Staff? What month and what year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: 1992, on the 9th of October. And there is a command, a written document about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this promotion was achieved in a period from '91 to '92. In addition to your experience from the JNA, did you complete any military schools in that period, that is '91, '92, '93?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: No. But all my life I was engaged in martial sports. I was interested in literature on the subject, including military literature from Japan, through Napoleon, the First and Second World Wars. And to facilitate my task -- I wish to point this out -- I had two of my closest associates, one of whom had graduated from the military academy, his name is Bruno Filipovic, and this other person, Dida Skokovic, who had a lot of military experience from the past war. They helped me in the structuring and the organisation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court what does HOS, H-O-S stand for, the letters?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Croatian Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who founded the HOS for the whole territory of the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: It was founded by the Croatian Party of Rights based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Croatian Party of Rights and the Supreme Commander of all HOS units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the commander and president of the Croatian Party of Rights and the Supreme Commander was Mr. Dobroslav Paraga.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was Chief of Staff of the war staff or the operative commander of HOS? There were several of them. There were changes.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: The first chief was Mr. Ante Paradzik. After his death the position was taken over by Dzapic, Prkacin and Mr. Dedakovic for a brief while, something didn't seem to work there, but these were the HOS commanders. The last commander was Mr. Ante Prkacin who also parted ways with the Supreme Commander Dobroslav Paraga later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, the HOS in Zenica, what was the composition of the fighters in terms of ethnic background during '92 and '93?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: The composition was always half/half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Half were, half were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The HOS in Zenica, who did it belong to? From the moment you joined HOS, and later on you left it, we will see later, but who -- under whose command were you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: According to the command -- to the order of the Supreme Commander of the Croatian Defence Forces, that is of HOS, we joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina by orders of Supreme Commander Dobroslav Paraga.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your particular case, that is you in Zenica, let us for a while leave aside the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Zenica, which unit of the BH army were you attached to during '92 and the beginning of ‘93? And please wait for me to finish my question, then a short pause to give the interpreters a chance to interpret my question and then we'll go on to your answer, and slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: We were attached to the 1st Zenica Brigade of the BH army -- or, rather, the Territorial Defence, which later became the BH army, and the commander of that unit was commander Dzemal Neitovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Later on, when the BH army was established when the Territorial Defence was transformed into what was known as the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what brigade were you to be attached to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: When the Territorial Defence was reorganised, we were attached to the 3rd Corps. That is the 314th Motorised Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your unit, therefore, belonged to the 3rd Corps of the BH army. And at what point in time, let us see the date first, did you decide to go over to the HVO and when did that process begin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Give us the dates first.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: My first thoughts about switching over to the HVO, my first serious thoughts along those lines, occurred towards the end of January, 1993, because there were increasing hostilities between Croats and Muslims, or, rather, there were some major incidents between them. Among those major incidents, I should like to mention that at the end of January in 1993, the massacre of Croats in Dusina, not far from Zenica, near the Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us when the decision was signed on the transfer of HOS units from the BH army to the HVO, on what date?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, 1993 we signed a document, or, rather, a decision whereby the HOS left the BH army and joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When was this decision published?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: The decision was published on the 10th of April, 1993. That is, five days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: At the time I was the coordinator between HOS units and HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Until the time hostilities started in Zenica, had that transformation been completed, or, rather, had you been organisationally inserted in the Jure Francetic Brigade, an HVO brigade or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: No. At that time I had just been informed that another brigade of the HVO was being formed which would exist on the right bank of the Bosna River. I was just informed that we would be attached to the Francetic Brigade as the 3rd Battalion, but I never received any document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we deduce then that at the time hostilities started between the HVO and the BH army, you had already abandoned the BH army but you had not become a part of the HVO structure; this was a kind of transitional period, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would now move on to another area. If you think now is a convenient time to adjourn ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone, Judge Jorda, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we still have another five minutes. The clock is fast here. So perhaps you can begin, unless it is a very broad subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We can. We will use up the remaining five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell their Honours now, after the events in Dusina, what was it that made you finally change your mind and leave the BH army and join the HVO? What were the additional reasons that were decisive for your decision?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: My people were being victimised, Croats were being killed, there was less and less safety for us in the town of Zenica. I can remember a few details. For example, the 7th Muslim Brigade, which was part of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, in the morning between 7.00 and 8.00 a.m., they had jogging exercises, footing drills. They were accommodated at Bilmista (phoen) where there was a training centre for the BH army, but this is far from the centre of the town, maybe two kilometres away, and every morning they would run through town singing nationalist songs. Let me try and recall some of them. "From Iran to the Bosnian doors, there will be no Serbs or Croats. We are waging war for Allah and against the infidels. A goose is on the Bosna river. This land will be Muslim land."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So these were songs that prompted you to decide. Did you have any intelligence reports indicating that conflicts could break out between the Croats and the Muslims or, rather, between the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did have some intelligence reports from officers in HOS, both Muslim and Croat, that 75 per cent of the BH army had been withdrawn from the battlefront, that only a quarter were facing the Serbs, and this could be seen in town because there were more and more troops in evidence in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your assumption regarding the 75 per cent of the army that had been withdrawn from the front into the territory under BH control? How did you think those troops would be used?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Intelligence reports said that the Muslim population had been expelled from many parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they were short of living space and that the area of the Croats in the Lasva River Valley had been promised to them. I also had intelligence reports that they wanted to capture the communication lines, "the Road of Salvation," as we called it, that went via Vranplanina to Tomislavgrad from where logistics supplies could be brought in and they wanted to gain control of it for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you inform your superiors, in the first place Supreme Commander Paraga, who throughout held the position that the Croats of HOS had to be in the BH army? Did you inform him about your suspicions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I personally got ready to travel. I took with me Matija Brajnovic, the coordinator of HOS, and my deputy, who is now deceased, Jordan Ostovic who was killed in the war, I took them to Zagreb because I would often report to Paraga about these events but I didn't meet with understanding, and I took with me these very prominent figures, the coordinator of HOS, who also coordinated with Paraga, and my own deputy. I took them there. I took with me a newspaper --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did you take them, and slow down, please? What town did you take them to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: I took them along this "Road of Salvation" to Zagreb, to the Ante Starcevic Centre where Dobroslav Paraga was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you say to Paraga?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: I presented all the problems I have just spoken about and I took with me a newspaper describing how many Croats had been killed. I remember the Kegelj family in particular. He looked at this and he said -- he said, "But is that possible?" And I said, "It's not just that. People cannot walk around freely." I reported about the 7th Muslim Brigade and, Your Honours, I told him that I would join the HVO, that the Croatian people were suffering, I had joined the war to defend the Croatian people, and I would continue to protect the Croatian people, every bird joins its flock, and I wanted to protect the Croats from any aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you wish, we can stop there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no. If you have another question, please proceed. I'm just trying to ask the witness to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have to slow down a lot because otherwise the Court will not hear what you're saying and we want the Court to understand what you're saying. Tell us, what was Paraga's reply? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN HOLMAN
utterances.text: Paraga continued to uphold the view that we should remain part of the BH army, but the vice-president, Mr. Ante Dzapic interceded and said, "Mr. President, we have to respect, acknowledge this report and attach much more significance to it because these people are coming directly from the field and they are reporting to us." And then I added to this that it was my -- that I had carried out my moral obligation, that I did not wish to betray the Supreme Commander but I wanted to be sure that I was morally correct by informing him that I would join the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, because my people were in jeopardy, and that that is what I would do regardless of his decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Holman, we asked you to come only for a short while, but we have to adjourn now. We will not be working next week, so you will be asked to come back on the 16th of November at 3.30, not at 2.00, because on the 16th of November, we have the welcoming of three new colleagues, Judges, who will be taking their solemn declarations, solemn oaths. Mr. Holman, thank you for coming, and we will be seeing you again on the 16th of November. Try, in the meantime, to train -- because you are a trainer -- try to practice to speak a little more slowly, if possible, for the benefit of our interpreters and for our own benefit, of course. Thank you. It's your sporting temperament that is pushing you on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for your patience. I apologise for speaking too quickly, but when I recall those wartime events, I tend to speak more quickly. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The hearing is adjourned

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of November, 1998, at 3.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
